reference.source: WHO Classification of Tumours: Digestive System Tumours
clinicalPearls: Most common mesenchymal tumour of the gastrointestinal tract, arising from the interstitial cells of Cajal or their precursors, most frequently in the stomach followed by the small intestine.
The great majority harbour activating mutations in KIT (CD117) or PDGFRA; immunohistochemistry for CD117 and DOG1 is the diagnostic cornerstone.

Small tumours are frequently incidental findings at endoscopy, imaging or surgery for another indication, whereas larger lesions present with occult or overt gastrointestinal bleeding, anaemia, abdominal mass or vague discomfort.

Risk stratification for malignant behaviour rests on tumour size, mitotic rate and anatomical site rather than a simple benign-versus-malignant dichotomy; small-bowel lesions behave more aggressively than gastric ones of equivalent size.

Endoscopic ultrasound shows a hypoechoic mass arising from the muscularis propria (fourth layer) and guides biopsy when tissue is needed; percutaneous biopsy of a resectable lesion is generally avoided owing to rupture and seeding risk.

Imatinib and successor tyrosine kinase inhibitors transformed management of advanced disease; response and drug selection are strongly mutation-dependent, and PDGFRA exon 18 D842V tumours are classically imatinib-resistant.

Wild-type GIST lacking KIT and PDGFRA mutations includes SDH-deficient tumours (often gastric, paediatric, associated with Carney triad and Carney-Stratakis syndrome) and NF1-associated and BRAF-mutant forms.

Complete surgical resection with an intact pseudocapsule and negative margins is the mainstay for localised disease; lymphadenectomy is not routinely required as nodal spread is uncommon except in SDH-deficient tumours.
reference.pathophysiology: Gastrointestinal stromal tumours arise from the interstitial cells of Cajal, the pacemaker cells that regulate gut peristalsis, or from their mesenchymal precursors within the wall of the tubular gastrointestinal tract. In most tumours a gain-of-function mutation in the receptor tyrosine kinase KIT drives ligand-independent, constitutive downstream signalling through the RAS-MAPK and PI3K-AKT pathways, promoting proliferation and survival; a minority are driven by analogous activating mutations in PDGFRA. A distinct subset lacks these mutations and instead shows loss of function of the succinate dehydrogenase complex, producing pseudohypoxic signalling, or is associated with neurofibromatosis type 1 or BRAF mutation. The specific driver dictates both morphology and, critically, sensitivity to tyrosine kinase inhibition, so molecular characterisation is integral to biological understanding and treatment.
additionalDifferentials: leiomyoma or leiomyosarcoma of the gut wall
additionalInvestigations: contrast-enhanced CT of the abdomen and pelvis for staging and response assessment
endoscopic ultrasound with fine-needle aspiration or biopsy
immunohistochemistry for CD117 (KIT), DOG1, CD34 and SDHB
molecular genotyping of KIT and PDGFRA (and BRAF/SDH where indicated)
assessment of mitotic count per defined high-power field area by histopathology
MRI for rectal or hepatic lesions where CT characterisation is limited
FDG-PET for early metabolic response to tyrosine kinase inhibitor therapy
redFlags: acute gastrointestinal haemorrhage or haemodynamic instability from a bleeding tumour
tumour rupture into the peritoneal cavity, markedly increasing recurrence risk
rapidly enlarging mass with new pain suggesting high-grade progression
signs of bowel obstruction or perforation
new hepatic or peritoneal lesions indicating metastatic spread
reference.prognosis: Prognosis depends chiefly on tumour size, mitotic rate, site and completeness of resection, with small gastric tumours often cured by excision while large small-bowel or ruptured tumours carry substantial recurrence risk. Tyrosine kinase inhibitors have markedly prolonged survival in advanced disease, though outcome varies with the underlying mutation.
pitfalls: Labelling a GIST as benign on size alone; small tumours can still metastasise and risk is a continuum.
Percutaneous biopsy of a readily resectable lesion, risking rupture and peritoneal seeding.
Failing to genotype before systemic therapy, leading to use of imatinib in resistant PDGFRA D842V tumours.
Misdiagnosing a CD117-negative or DOG1-positive tumour as leiomyoma or schwannoma without full immunohistochemistry.
Overlooking SDH-deficient GIST in young patients and its associated syndromic and nodal-spread implications.

management: Confirm diagnosis by core needle biopsy and perform KIT/PDGFRA mutational analysis (with SDH immunohistochemistry if both negative) before planning medical therapy, since genotype predicts prognosis and drug sensitivity.

For localized disease, surgery with macroscopically complete (R0) resection is the mainstay; tumours 2 cm or larger should generally be resected, small 1 to 2 cm lesions may be observed or resected, and rupture or capsule violation during surgery must be avoided given its adverse prognostic impact.

Consider preoperative (neoadjuvant) imatinib to shrink a large or high rupture risk tumour before surgery, only after confirming an imatinib-sensitive genotype, monitoring response clinically and radiologically.

Offer adjuvant imatinib, typically for about three years, to patients with a sufficiently high estimated relapse risk after complete resection, restricted to imatinib-sensitive genotypes (KIT-mutated or PDGFRA-mutated excluding D842V and related exon 18 variants).
For metastatic or unresectable disease, start indefinite TKI therapy rather than a fixed course, since stopping typically leads to progression within months.

Sequence systemic therapy by line: imatinib first for imatinib-sensitive genotypes (with avapritinib instead for PDGFRA D842V and related exon 18 mutations), then sunitinib, then regorafenib, then ripretinib as later lines for progressive disease.
Consider dose escalation of the current TKI at progression in some patients, as this can produce temporary benefit, and check adherence before attributing progression to molecular resistance.
For SDH-deficient GIST, which is essentially imatinib-insensitive, consider sunitinib or regorafenib given the more indolent natural history of this subtype.

For limited or focal progression on an otherwise responding TKI, consider continuing the current TKI while using surgery or ablation to control the progressing focus, recognizing this is not backed by prospective trial data.

Consider surgical resection of residual imatinib-responding metastatic disease only when complete resection of all visible disease is feasible, continuing the TKI afterward regardless of how complete resection appears, since its prognostic benefit is unproven.
Reserve radiotherapy for palliation, such as extra-abdominal (bone) metastases, since it has no established curative role in GIST.

Follow up after curative surgery with periodic CT of the abdomen (MRI as an alternative) to detect peritoneal or liver relapse, without routine endoscopy, focusing surveillance on the highest-risk two to three year window after surgery or adjuvant therapy.

On TKI therapy, follow response with periodic cross-sectional imaging, using FDG-PET selectively for early response or resistance signals, and refer to a multidisciplinary sarcoma/GIST team for neoadjuvant candidates, syndromic or resistant genotypes, rectal or periampullary GIST, and decisions about surgery for residual metastatic disease.
